lead: AC power has two parts. The real part, P, does useful work and becomes heat, light or torque. The reactive part, Q, only swings energy between the source and the load's electric or magnetic field. Together they form complex power S = P + jQ; its magnitude is apparent power, measured in volt-amperes. This idea lets you size cables and generators, read an electricity bill, and correct a low power factor with a capacitor.
prereq: You need RMS values from 3.1, the impedance angle from 3.3, and phasor V and I from 3.4.

blocks.text: With v(t)=V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt+θ<sub>v</sub>) and i(t)=I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt+θ<sub>i</sub>), instantaneous power is p(t)=v(t)i(t). Let φ=θ<sub>v</sub>−θ<sub>i</sub>. Using sin A sin B = ½[cos(A−B)−cos(A+B)] gives
p(t) = Vrms Irms cos φ − Vrms Irms cos(2ωt + θv + θi)
V<sub>m</sub>, I<sub>m</sub> are peak volts and amps; V<sub>rms</sub>=V<sub>m</sub>/√2 and I<sub>rms</sub>=I<sub>m</sub>/√2; ω=2πf; φ=θ<sub>v</sub>−θ<sub>i</sub> is the impedance angle.

The second term has frequency 2f, so power pulses twice per supply cycle, and its average over a cycle is zero. The average is P = V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> cos φ, in watts (W). A positive P means net energy flows from source to load. When cos φ < 1, p(t) goes negative for part of each cycle, and energy flows back to the source. The figure draws the motor of the worked example (230 V, 10 A, φ = 36.87°): p(t) swings between P − |S| = 1840 − 2300 = −460 W and P + |S| = 4140 W and averages 1840 W. The pulsation can be split in two: p(t) = P(1 − cos 2α) − Q sin 2α, with α = ωt + θ<sub>v</sub>. The first part never goes negative; it is real power arriving in pulses, and a pure resistor has only this part. The second part, with peak Q, is energy flowing into the inductance or capacitance and back, and it averages zero. Only resistance absorbs real power: P = Irms² R.

Reactive power is Q=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> sinφ, in volt-ampere reactive (VAR). It is not heat; it is the peak rate at which energy is exchanged with inductance or capacitance. It is a power, not an energy, so its unit is VAR and never joule. By convention, an inductive load has current lagging voltage, φ>0, so Q is positive. A capacitive load has current leading, φ<0, so Q is negative. Apparent power is |S|=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub>, in volt-ampere (VA). It is the product of RMS readings and sets the current a cable must carry. Complex power is S=V I*, where I* is the complex conjugate of the current phasor and V is the voltage phasor. With V=V<sub>rms</sub>∠0 and I=I<sub>rms</sub>∠−φ, S=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub>∠φ=P+jQ.
P = |S| cosφ, Q = |S| sinφ, |S| = √(P² + Q²), φ = tan⁻¹(Q/P)
blocks.where: P is real power in W; Q is reactive power in VAR; |S| is apparent power in VA; φ is the power-factor angle; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: The power triangle is a right triangle with P on the adjacent side, Q on the opposite side and |S| on the hypotenuse. Across parallel branches, real powers add and reactive powers add with sign: P<sub>total</sub>=ΣP, Q<sub>total</sub>=ΣQ. Apparent powers do not add arithmetically. Two loads of 100 VA each at different power factors give |S<sub>total</sub>|=√(P<sub>total</sub>²+Q<sub>total</sub>²), not 200 VA unless their power factors are equal and of the same sign (both lagging or both leading).

Power factor is cosφ=P/|S|, the cosine of the angle between voltage and current; for a series circuit it also equals R/|Z|. It is called lagging when current lags voltage (inductive) and leading when current leads voltage (capacitive). A low power factor means a larger current for the same P, so cables, transformers and switchgear must be bigger, and losses I²R rise. Utilities therefore charge industrial consumers for poor power factor; the exact tariff varies. Correction means adding a parallel capacitor that supplies Q<sub>C</sub> while P stays the same. For a load Q<sub>1</sub> at φ<sub>1</sub> changed to Q<sub>2</sub> at φ<sub>2</sub>, Q<sub>C</sub>=Q<sub>1</sub>−Q<sub>2</sub>=P(tanφ1−tanφ2). The capacitor is C=Q<sub>C</sub>/(ωVrms²), with V<sub>rms</sub> the supply voltage and ω=2πf. The capacitor's own reactive power is −Q<sub>C</sub>, so it cancels part of the inductive Q. After correction the apparent power falls from P/cosφ1 to P/cosφ2, but the real power P is unchanged. The supply current falls because it carries less reactive component. This is why a factory can avoid a penalty without changing its machines.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a motor taking 10 A at 0.8 power factor lagging. Find the real power P, the reactive power Q and the apparent power |S|. Find the parallel capacitor that raises the power factor to 0.95 lagging.
steps: Real power: P=|S| cosφ1=2300×0.8=1840 W. Also φ<sub>1</sub>=acos(0.8)=36.87°.
Reactive power: Q<sub>1</sub>=|S| sinφ1=2300×0.6=1380 VAR. It is positive because the load is inductive and lagging.
At the new power factor 0.95: φ<sub>2</sub>=acos(0.95)=18.19°. The real power stays 1840 W, so Q<sub>2</sub>=P tanφ2=1840×0.3287=604.8 VAR.
The capacitor value is 46.6 µF, connected in parallel with the motor.
examples.answer: P=1840 W, Q<sub>1</sub>=1380 VAR, |S|=2300 VA, and C≈46.6 µF raises the power factor to 0.95 lagging.
examples.check:
import math
V = 230.0
I = 10.0
f = 50.0
pf1 = 0.8
pf2 = 0.95
S = V * I
P = S * pf1
phi1 = math.acos(pf1)
Q1 = S * math.sin(phi1)
phi2 = math.acos(pf2)
Q2 = P * math.tan(phi2)
Qc = Q1 - Q2
w = 2 * math.pi * f
C = Qc / (w * V**2)
print(int(round(S)))
print(int(round(P)))
print(int(round(Q1)))
print(round(Q2, 1))
print(round(Qc, 1))
print(round(C * 1e6, 1))

traps: Using peak values in V I: average power uses RMS. For a sine, V<sub>rms</sub>=V<sub>m</sub>/√2, so P=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> cosφ=(V<sub>m</sub> I<sub>m</sub>/2)cosφ.
Adding apparent powers: 100 VA at 0.6 pf plus 100 VA at 0.8 pf is not 200 VA. Add P and Q separately, then |S|=√(P²+Q²).
Getting the sign of Q wrong: inductive lagging has Q positive; capacitive leading has Q negative. A capacitor's Q<sub>C</sub> is negative in the sum S<sub>load</sub>+S<sub>C</sub>.
Forgetting that power-factor correction leaves P unchanged: the capacitor changes Q and line current, not the motor's watts.
Mixing units: W for P, VAR for Q, VA for |S|. Do not write VAR for apparent power or W for reactive power.

quiz.q: Define real, reactive and apparent power, with their units.
quiz.a: P=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> cosφ in W; Q=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> sinφ in VAR; |S|=V<sub>rms</sub> I<sub>rms</sub> in VA.

quiz.q: Why can instantaneous power be negative for part of a cycle when the power factor is less than one?
quiz.a: The load stores energy in inductance or capacitance and returns some of it to the source during part of each cycle. The average real power is still positive for a normal load.

quiz.q: A load takes 120 V, 5 A and 480 W. Find |S|, power factor and the magnitude of Q.
quiz.a: |S|=120×5=600 VA. pf=480/600=0.8. |Q|=√(600²−480²)=360 VAR. Q is positive if the load is lagging.

quiz.q: Two loads are in parallel: 100 VA at 0.6 pf lagging and 100 VA at 0.8 pf lagging. Find total P, total Q, |S<sub>total</sub>| and overall power factor.
quiz.a: Load 1: P1=60 W, Q<sub>1</sub>=80 VAR. Load 2: P2=80 W, Q<sub>2</sub>=60 VAR. Total P=140 W, Q=140 VAR. |S<sub>total</sub>|=√(140²+140²)=197.99 VA. pf=140/197.99=0.707 lagging.

quiz.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz load takes 8 A at 0.7 power factor lagging. Find the capacitor needed to raise the power factor to 0.9 lagging.
Why does a low power factor increase electricity cost for an industry even if the real power P is the same?
quiz.a: For the same P, a lower power factor needs a larger current. Cables, transformers and switchgear must be larger, and I²R losses are higher. Utilities also apply a power-factor penalty or tariff; the exact tariff varies.

quiz.q: State the complex power formula and say what I* means.
quiz.a: S=V I*, where V and I are RMS phasors and I* is the complex conjugate of I. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power-factor correction is standard in industrial electrical design; capacitor banks switch in steps as motor load changes. Modern grid work adds harmonics and distortion power, so apparent power is split into fundamental and non-fundamental parts. Search next for power-factor correction, static VAR compensators and distortion power.

figure.caption: Top: instantaneous power of the worked example's motor. It pulses at 100 Hz between −460 W and 4140 W and averages P = 1840 W. Bottom: its power triangle; the 46.6 µF capacitor cancels 775.2 var, so the triangle flattens from pf 0.80 to 0.95 while P stays the same.

spec.aria: Top: p(t) over 20 ms swinging from minus 460 W to 4140 W around an average of 1840 W. Bottom: power triangle with P 1840 W, Q falling from 1380 var to 604.8 var after a 775.2 var capacitor, apparent power from 2300 to 1937 VA.
